challenge.say: This is the Moon, seen from above its south pole. A lander there needs two things from the sky: the Sun, for power, and Earth, for a direct radio link. It is nothing like Earth: the Moon turns once a month, and near its pole the Sun and Earth never climb. They skim the horizon, so the hills decide when each is in view.

plan.say: The front page is the Moon to watch. Plan a landing starts a plan, and a plan begins with two choices. Where: a listed site, from Apollo to NASA's commercial landers, other countries' landers and future targets, or any point on the Moon, by its coordinates. And when: a date and hour, in UTC. Ours is Connecting Ridge, on the sixth of May 2027.

verdict.say: So, does it fit? The answer comes first. This landing does not, and Sightline says why: the Sun is down for ninety-five hours and Earth is out of view for a hundred and sixty-nine, against a limit of a day each. Under it are the numbers: the Sun's elevation, a key measure for power, and its share of the mission; Earth, the same way; and the ground's slope.

slipped.say: Now the real problem: launch dates slip. Sightline names the next landing that fits. One press, and it is in the plan beside the first, as scenario B: the same site, on the twenty-second of June, nearly seven weeks later, with a green verdict. In separate tools, that means starting again in each one.

skyline.say: So why does it not fit? One window faces the Sun, the other Earth, over the real skyline, traced from NASA's laser-measured terrain. Both are low, and each counts down: sunset in five and a half days, Earthset in seven. Seen from the Moon, Earth stays in one place; near the pole that place is the skyline, so here it sets.

time.say: Now run the mission forward. Gold is the Sun, blue is Earth, green is both. The frame marks the fourteen days, and the gaps inside it are the verdict's reasons: the Sun gone for four days, Earth gone for the whole second week. Play it, or step back to a day, a month or a year. Over a year the pattern shifts: the Moon has seasons too.

ground.say: Now look at the ground itself. Three views show the same hour: the whole Moon from orbit, the site close up, and the surface. Layers puts NASA's own maps over the ground: photos, steep ground, permanent shadow, temperature. And every plan opens in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, so anyone can check.

compare.say: Waiting is one answer. Would moving be another? Compare sets the scenarios side by side: A failed, B is the later date, and C and D are two other sites near the pole on the original date. Neither fits, though one is sunlit for two thirds of the mission and the other for a seventh. A star marks the best in each row; there is no blended score.

planner.say: So was May ever possible? The Planner steps back to every listed site against every month, counting the days with a landing that fits. In May 2027, none of the four ridge sites at the pole has one. In June, Connecting Ridge has three. A site that never fits says which limit blocks it.

accuracy.say: We chose B. But no lander comes down exactly on its mark. B fits on its aim point, and yet, of the touchdowns within about a hundred meters of it, only thirty-eight percent would. Landing accuracy shows what goes wrong in the rest, and offers a better aim: forty-four meters away, where sixty percent fit. Near the pole, a few meters matter.

trust.say: Can it be trusted? Every number is computed from public NASA data by our own code, then checked against NASA three ways. The positions are compared with JPL Horizons at every hour. The long-run sunlight, with NASA's own map. And the model, with dated photos taken from orbit. The Guide tells that story for a first-time visitor, and says plainly what Sightline cannot tell you.

scout.say: Or just ask. Scout takes a question in plain words and looks the answer up in the same data the screen uses. He is an AI, and he is never allowed to write a number himself: the server fills in every figure, so what he says matches what you see.

scenarios.say: The plan now holds two options, each with a letter: A, the first landing, and B, the later one. A letter is one scenario: a site and a landing hour. The plus adds another, up to four. There: scenario C. Change its site or date, and the whole screen answers for it. The minus on a letter drops it, and Undo brings it back.

mission.say: The third choice is the mission: what it must survive. A short stay is fourteen days, with at most a day of darkness, at most a day of radio silence, the Sun and Earth in view at landing, and ground no steeper than ten degrees. In view means any part of the disc above the skyline. That is generous for a radio link, so Advanced can ask for Earth's center to stand two or five degrees clear.

handon.say: Last, hand it on paper. Brief writes the scenario on show out in full, to read or print: the month's landing days, this landing, and what follows it. That was the story. Every feature has a short guide of its own, listed in the Guide, and some panels offer theirs as Show me how. Try the one on Canada's utility rover, a real mission, or start planning your own.

depth.say: Four scenarios, one decision. The Planner's Compare tab sets them against each other in full. At a glance is one row a scenario, each figure colored by your limits: within them, close to one, or past it. Under it is the whole table: the angles at landing, power, radio and the ground. Only B fits, so B goes forward. And Export saves that table, or every hour of the mission, as a file for your own tools.

share.say: Now send it to someone. Share opens a short list. The plan is already a link: the address holds every scenario, with its site and landing hour, and the mission's limits, so whoever opens it sees the same plan. Copy link puts that address on your clipboard. Save with a name keeps it under a short link, and lists it in the Library.
